title: Kaposi's sarcoma
description: Cancer of the skin, integumentary lymph nodes, or other organs
wiki_lead:
Kaposi's sarcoma (KS) is a type of cancer that can form masses on the skin, in lymph nodes, in the mouth, or in other organs. The skin lesions are usually painless, purple, and may be flat or raised. Lesions can occur singly, multiply in a limited area, or may be widespread. Depending on the sub-type of disease and level of immune suppression, KS may worsen either gradually or quickly. Except for classic KS where there is generally no immune suppression, KS is caused by a combination of immune suppression (such as HIV/AIDS) and infection by Human herpesvirus 8 (HHV8 – also called KS-associated herpesvirus (KSHV)).
Classic, endemic, immunosuppression therapy-related (also known as iatrogenic), and epidemic (also known as AIDS-related) sub-types are all described. Classic KS tends to affect older men in regions where KSHV is highly prevalent (Mediterranean, Eastern Europe, Middle East), is usually slow-growing, and most often affects only the legs. Endemic KS is most common in Sub-Saharan Africa and is more aggressive in children, while older adults present similarly to classic KS. Immunosuppression therapy-related KS generally occurs in people following organ transplantation and mostly affects the skin. Epidemic KS occurs in people with AIDS and many parts of the body can be affected. KS is diagnosed by tissue biopsy, while the extent of disease may be determined by medical imaging.
Treatment is based on the sub-type, whether the condition is localized or widespread, and the person's immune function. Localized skin lesions may be treated by surgery, injections of chemotherapy into the lesion, or radiation therapy. Widespread disease may be treated with chemotherapy or biologic therapy. In those with HIV/AIDS, highly active antiretroviral therapy (HAART) prevents and often treats KS. In certain cases the addition of chemotherapy may be required. With widespread disease, death may occur.
The condition is relatively common in people with HIV/AIDS and following organ transplants. Over 35% of people with AIDS may be affected. KS was first described by Moritz Kaposi in 1872, but the name was coined only in 1891. It became more widely known as one of the AIDS-defining illnesses in the 1980s. KSHV was discovered as a causative agent in 1994.

Signs and symptoms
KS lesions are nodules or blotches that may be red, purple, brown, or black, and are usually papular.
They are typically found on the skin, but spread elsewhere is common, especially the mouth, gastrointestinal tract, and respiratory tract. Growth can range from very slow to explosively fast and is associated with significant mortality and morbidity.
The lesions are painless but become cosmetically disfiguring or interruptive to organs.

grok_lead: Kaposi's sarcoma (KS) is a multifocal angioproliferative neoplasm caused by human herpesvirus 8 (HHV-8), also known as Kaposi sarcoma-associated herpesvirus (KSHV), presenting as reddish-purple vascular lesions on the skin, mucous membranes, lymph nodes, or internal organs. The tumor arises from endothelial and spindle cells in the context of HHV-8 infection combined with immunosuppression or other cofactors, with HHV-8 DNA detectable in over 90% of lesions across all variants. First described in 1872 by Hungarian dermatologist Moritz Kaposi as "idiopathic multiple pigmented sarcoma," KS manifests in four epidemiological forms: classic (indolent, affecting elderly men of Mediterranean, Middle Eastern, or Jewish ancestry), endemic (prevalent in sub-Saharan Africa, often involving children and lymphadenopathic disease), iatrogenic (in organ transplant recipients on immunosuppressive therapy), and epidemic or AIDS-associated (historically aggressive in HIV-infected individuals prior to antiretroviral therapy). While rare globally outside high-prevalence regions, KS incidence surged in the early 1980s with the HIV/AIDS epidemic, highlighting its dependence on T-cell immunodeficiency, though HHV-8 seroprevalence alone does not invariably lead to malignancy without additional triggers like cytokine dysregulation or HIV-induced immune collapse. Treatment typically involves addressing underlying immunosuppression, with chemotherapy reserved for advanced visceral disease, reflecting KS's variable prognosis from indolent cutaneous patches to disseminated fatal involvement.
